# Centered factorial effects and equivalent Gaussian parameterizations

This offline packet contains the statistical definitions needed to interpret
the supplied calibration workflow. It is based on the version-matched PyMC
distribution documentation, the PyMC3 framework paper, and the Stan User's
Guide discussion of centered vectors.

## 1. Factorial calibration model

Suppose laboratories `l = 1, ..., L` measure the same response under protocols
`p = 1, ..., P`. A two-way Gaussian effects model can be written as

$$
y_{lp} \sim
\mathcal{N}(\mu + a_l + b_p + g_{lp}, s_{lp}),
$$

where `mu` is the grand mean, `a_l` is a laboratory effect, `b_p` is a
protocol effect, `g_lp` is a laboratory-by-protocol interaction, and `s_lp`
is the known standard error of the observed cell summary.

Without identifying constraints, constants can be moved between the grand mean
and the main effects without changing fitted responses. A common convention is

$$
\sum_{l=1}^{L} a_l = 0,
\qquad
\sum_{p=1}^{P} b_p = 0.
$$

The interaction represents only the non-additive part of the response when it
is centered across both axes:

$$
\sum_{l=1}^{L} g_{lp} = 0 \quad \text{for every } p,
\qquad
\sum_{p=1}^{P} g_{lp} = 0 \quad \text{for every } l.
$$

These constraints define the interpretation of the effects. They are not
additional observations.

## 2. Documented centered Gaussian distribution

The source-version PyMC documentation describes `ZeroSumNormal` as a centered
Gaussian distribution for which one or more selected trailing axes sum to zero.
For one constrained axis of length `K`, the covariance is

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(x) =
\sigma^2\left(I - \frac{1}{K}J\right),
$$

where `I` is the identity matrix and every entry of `J` is one. The parameter
`sigma` is the standard deviation of the underlying unconstrained Normal used
by the construction. In this source version it is a positive scalar.

By default the rightmost axis is constrained. The public API can constrain more
than one trailing axis. A matrix constrained over its last two axes therefore
has zero sums along both of those axes.

## 3. Orthonormal reduced coordinates

A zero-sum vector can be represented without redundancy. Let the columns of
`B` form an orthonormal basis for the subspace perpendicular to the all-ones
vector:

$$
B^T B = I,
\qquad
B^T \mathbf{1} = 0.
$$

If

$$
z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I),
\qquad
x = Bz,
$$

then `x` has the centered covariance above and lies on the zero-sum support.
Subtracting the mean from an unconstrained Gaussian vector is another way to
construct the same covariance.

For a two-way interaction, bases for the laboratory and protocol centered
subspaces can be combined to represent exactly the matrices whose row and
column sums are zero.

## 4. Reparameterization coherence

A full constrained representation and an orthonormal reduced-coordinate
representation are two coordinate systems for the same statistical model. In a
linear-Gaussian analysis with the same priors, observations, and standard
errors, they must produce the same posterior fitted responses and the same
posterior summaries for any fixed linear contrast, up to numerical and Monte
Carlo error.

This statement does not depend on a particular optimizer or sampler. Different
computational paths may represent the model differently internally, but they do
not define different prior shrinkage or different scientific contrasts.

## 5. Planned interaction contrasts

A difference-in-differences contrast compares a protocol change between two
laboratories. For laboratories `l_1`, `l_2` and protocols `p_1`, `p_2`,
one example is

$$
C =
(\eta_{l_1 p_1} - \eta_{l_1 p_2})
-
(\eta_{l_2 p_1} - \eta_{l_2 p_2}),
$$

where `eta_lp = mu + a_l + b_p + g_lp` is the fitted response. Additive grand,
laboratory, and protocol contributions cancel, so this contrast isolates a
laboratory-by-protocol interaction.

Posterior means estimate the interaction contrast. Posterior standard
deviations and intervals quantify uncertainty. Both are properties of the
declared probability model.

## 6. Sources

- Salvatier, Wiecki, and Fonnesbeck, "Probabilistic programming in Python using
  PyMC3," *PeerJ Computer Science* 2:e55 (2016), DOI
  [10.7717/peerj-cs.55](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.55).
- PyMC documentation, `ZeroSumNormal` distribution API:
  [pymc.ZeroSumNormal](https://www.pymc.io/projects/docs/en/stable/api/distributions/generated/pymc.ZeroSumNormal.html).
- Stan User's Guide, "Parameterizing centered vectors":
  [centered-vector parameterization](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/regression.html#parameterizing-centered-vectors).
- Matching source-version documentation is retained in
  `source/pymc/distributions/multivariate.py`.

These sources define the support, covariance, parameter meaning, model
identifiability, and equivalence needed for the investigation. They do not
prescribe a source-level repair.
# Public reproduction

Run the centered factorial-effects workflow with:

```bash
python reproduce.py
```

The script reads the fixed offline study in
`fixtures/factorial_calibration_study.json`. It builds one Gaussian model with
laboratory, protocol, and laboratory-by-protocol effects, runs bounded
fixed-seed posterior sampling, and evaluates three pre-planned interaction
contrasts.

It writes:

```text
outputs/public_reproduction_report.json
```

The report contains finite sample counts, zero-sum residuals, and posterior
contrast means and standard deviations observed from the candidate model. It
does not contain fixed expected summaries or evaluate an analytic probability
density.

The report uses three statuses:

- `workflow_completed`: the candidate model produced finite posterior
  observations and constraint diagnostics; this is not a correctness claim;
- `pre_fix_expected_failure`: the model ran but did not produce a usable finite
  observation; and
- `runner_failure`: imports, fixture validation, model construction, sampling,
  extraction, shape checks, or report generation failed before a usable
  scientific comparison existed.

The public command is a diagnostic workbench. Authoritative distribution
comparisons and unseen-shape coverage are implemented in the private verifier.
# Restore coherent inference in a centered factorial-effects model

A collaborative assay-calibration workflow uses the supplied PyMC source
snapshot to analyze measurements from several laboratories and protocols. The
Gaussian model contains centered laboratory effects, centered protocol effects,
and a centered laboratory-by-protocol interaction. The public workflow exposes
posterior observations and the declared identifying constraints; the verifier
checks the distribution semantics across additional shapes, scales, and
support configurations.

Run `python reproduce.py` to reproduce the scientific discrepancy. Read the
supplied method material, inspect the complete source snapshot, and repair the
implementation so that the posterior calculation represents the documented
model for all supported inputs. Preserve the public distribution API and the
meaning of its scale and support. The repair must generalize beyond the public
laboratories, protocols, data matrix, prior scales, sampling seed, and reported
contrasts.

Do not modify `reproduce.py`, `reproduction.md`, the fixture, task metadata,
or the evaluation harness. Generated files belong under `outputs/`.

# Architecture
This document describes the high-level architecture of PyMC.

# Bird's Eye View
[comment]: <> (https://drive.google.com/file/d/1lfEzokkNUJr_JIeSDQfha5a57pokz0qI)
![Architecture](docs/Architecture.png)
Lets you define probabilistic graphs or models that can be easily used to compute log probabilities for posterior
inference or to draw random samples for prior and posterior prediction.

PyMC includes a few inference techniques, in particular:
* Markov chain Monte Carlo
* Variational Inference
* Sequential Monte Carlo

It also contains numerous others pieces of functionality such as GraphviZ model visualization tools
as well as various mathematical helper functions.

The most central pieces functionality of PyMC are shown visually below, as well as their
relation to other major packages. Not all modules are shown, either because
they are smaller or self explanatory in scope, or they're pending
deprecation

## Functionality not in PyMC
It is easier to start with functionality that is not present in PyMC but
rather deferred to outside libraries. If seeking to understand any
of the topics below refer to that specific library

### PyTensor
* Gradient computation
* Random number generation
* Low level tensor operation definition
* Low level operation graphs

### ArviZ
* Plotting e.g. Trace plots, rank plots, posterior plots
* MCMC sampling diagnostics e.g. Rhat, Effective Sample Size.
* Model comparison, particularly efficient leave-one-out cross-validation approximation
* Inference Data structure


# Modules
The codebase of PyMC is split among single Python file modules at the root
level, as well as directories with Python code for logical groups of functionality.
Admittedly the split between single `.py` module or directory is not defined by a strict
criteria but tends to occur when single `.py` files would be "too big".
We will with the modules needed implement "simple MCMC" model shown below
before detailing the remaining modules, such as Variational Inference, Ordinary Differential Equations,
or Sequential Monte Carlo.

```python
with pm.Model() as model:
  theta = pm.Beta("theta", alpha=1, beta=2)
  p = pm.Beta("n", p=theta, n=2, observed=[1,2])
  inf_data = pm.sample()


```

## {mod}`pymc.model`
Contains primitives related model definition and methods used for evaluation of the model.
In no particular order they are

* `ContextMeta`: The context manager that enables the `with pm.Model() as model` syntax
* {class}`~pymc.Factor`: Defines the methods for the various logprobs for models
* `ValueGrad` which handles the value and gradient and is the main connection point to PyTensor
* `Deterministic` and `Potential`: Definitions for two pieces of functionality useful in some model definitions

## distributions/
Contains multiple submodules that define distributions,  as well as logic that aids in distributions usage.
Important modules to note are

* `distribution.py`: This contains parent class for all PyMC distributions.
  Notably the `distribution.distribution` class contains the `observed` argument which in PyMC differentiates
  a random variable distribution from a likelihood distribution.

* `logprob.py`: This contains the log probability logic for the distributions themselves.
  The log probability calculation is deferred to PyTensor

* `dist_math.py`: Various convenience operators for distributions.
  This includes mathematical operators such as `logpower` or `all_true`methods.
  It also contains a suite of lognormal methods and transformation methods

## /sampling.py
Interface to posterior, prior predictive, and posterior sampling as well as various methods to identify and initialize
stepper methods. Also contains logic to check for "all continuous" variables and initialize NUTS

## step_methods/
Contains various step methods for various sampling algorithms, such as MCMC, and SMC. `step_methods.hmc` includes
the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling methods as well as helper functions such as the integrators used for those methods

## tests/
All tests for testing functionality of codebase. All modules prefixed with `test_` are tests themselves, whereas all
other modules contain various supporting code such as fixtures, configurations, etc

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any


TASK_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
SOURCE_DIR = TASK_DIR / "source"
OUTPUT_DIR = TASK_DIR / "outputs"
FIXTURE_PATH = TASK_DIR / "fixtures" / "factorial_calibration_study.json"


def load_case() -> dict[str, Any]:
    case = json.loads(FIXTURE_PATH.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    required = {
        "case_name",
        "laboratories",
        "protocols",
        "cell_estimates",
        "cell_standard_errors",
        "prior_scales",
        "sampling",
        "planned_contrasts",
    }
    missing = sorted(required - set(case))
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"fixture is missing fields: {', '.join(missing)}")
    return case


def finite_matrix(np, value: object, shape: tuple[int, int], field: str):
    matrix = np.asarray(value, dtype=float)
    if matrix.shape != shape:
        raise ValueError(f"{field} must have shape {shape}, got {matrix.shape}")
    if not np.all(np.isfinite(matrix)):
        raise ValueError(f"{field} contains non-finite values")
    return matrix


def validate_case(np, case: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    laboratories = list(case["laboratories"])
    protocols = list(case["protocols"])
    if len(laboratories) < 3 or len(protocols) < 3:
        raise ValueError("the study requires at least three laboratories and protocols")
    if len(set(laboratories)) != len(laboratories):
        raise ValueError("laboratory names must be unique")
    if len(set(protocols)) != len(protocols):
        raise ValueError("protocol names must be unique")

    shape = (len(laboratories), len(protocols))
    cell_estimates = finite_matrix(np, case["cell_estimates"], shape, "cell_estimates")
    cell_standard_errors = finite_matrix(
        np,
        case["cell_standard_errors"],
        shape,
        "cell_standard_errors",
    )
    if np.any(cell_standard_errors <= 0):
        raise ValueError("cell_standard_errors must be positive")

    prior_scales = dict(case["prior_scales"])
    for field in ("grand_mean", "laboratory", "protocol", "interaction"):
        value = float(prior_scales[field])
        if not np.isfinite(value) or value <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f"prior scale {field} must be positive and finite")
        prior_scales[field] = value

    sampling = dict(case["sampling"])
    for field in ("draws", "tune", "chains", "cores", "seed"):
        sampling[field] = int(sampling[field])
    sampling["target_accept"] = float(sampling["target_accept"])
    if sampling["draws"] < 100 or sampling["tune"] < 0:
        raise ValueError("sampling settings are not sufficient for the public workflow")
    if sampling["chains"] != 1 or sampling["cores"] != 1:
        raise ValueError("the public workflow requires one bounded chain and core")
    if not 0.5 < sampling["target_accept"] < 1.0:
        raise ValueError("target_accept must lie between 0.5 and 1.0")

    laboratory_index = {name: index for index, name in enumerate(laboratories)}
    protocol_index = {name: index for index, name in enumerate(protocols)}
    planned_contrasts = list(case["planned_contrasts"])
    if not planned_contrasts:
        raise ValueError("at least one planned contrast is required")

    normalized_contrasts: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    contrast_names: set[str] = set()
    for contrast in planned_contrasts:
        name = str(contrast["name"])
        if not name or name in contrast_names:
            raise ValueError("planned contrast names must be non-empty and unique")
        contrast_names.add(name)

        terms = list(contrast["terms"])
        if len(terms) < 2:
            raise ValueError(f"contrast {name} requires at least two terms")
        normalized_terms = []
        coefficient_sum = 0.0
        for term in terms:
            laboratory = str(term["laboratory"])
            protocol = str(term["protocol"])
            if laboratory not in laboratory_index:
                raise ValueError(f"contrast {name} uses unknown laboratory {laboratory}")
            if protocol not in protocol_index:
                raise ValueError(f"contrast {name} uses unknown protocol {protocol}")
            coefficient = float(term["coefficient"])
            if not np.isfinite(coefficient):
                raise ValueError(f"contrast {name} has a non-finite coefficient")
            coefficient_sum += coefficient
            normalized_terms.append(
                {
                    "laboratory": laboratory,
                    "protocol": protocol,
                    "laboratory_index": laboratory_index[laboratory],
                    "protocol_index": protocol_index[protocol],
                    "coefficient": coefficient,
                }
            )
        if not np.isclose(coefficient_sum, 0.0, atol=1e-12, rtol=0.0):
            raise ValueError(f"contrast {name} coefficients must sum to zero")

        normalized_contrasts.append(
            {
                "name": name,
                "terms": normalized_terms,
            }
        )

    return {
        "case_name": str(case["case_name"]),
        "laboratories": laboratories,
        "protocols": protocols,
        "cell_estimates": cell_estimates,
        "cell_standard_errors": cell_standard_errors,
        "prior_scales": prior_scales,
        "sampling": sampling,
        "planned_contrasts": normalized_contrasts,
    }


def flatten_posterior(np, posterior, variable: str, trailing_shape: tuple[int, ...]):
    values = np.asarray(posterior[variable], dtype=float)
    expected_ndim = 2 + len(trailing_shape)
    if values.ndim != expected_ndim:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"posterior variable {variable} has ndim {values.ndim}, expected {expected_ndim}"
        )
    if trailing_shape and tuple(values.shape[-len(trailing_shape) :]) != trailing_shape:
        raise RuntimeError(
            f"posterior variable {variable} has trailing shape "
            f"{values.shape[-len(trailing_shape):]}, expected {trailing_shape}"
        )
    reshaped = values.reshape((-1,) + trailing_shape) if trailing_shape else values.reshape(-1)
    if reshaped.shape[0] < 2:
        raise RuntimeError(f"posterior variable {variable} has too few samples")
    if not np.all(np.isfinite(reshaped)):
        raise RuntimeError(f"posterior variable {variable} contains non-finite samples")
    return reshaped


def summarize_contrast(np, values) -> dict[str, float]:
    return {
        "mean": float(np.mean(values)),
        "sd": float(np.std(values, ddof=1)),
        "interval_90": [
            float(np.quantile(values, 0.05)),
            float(np.quantile(values, 0.95)),
        ],
    }


def run_workflow(pm, np, raw_case: dict[str, Any]) -> dict[str, Any]:
    case = validate_case(np, raw_case)
    laboratories = case["laboratories"]
    protocols = case["protocols"]
    n_laboratories = len(laboratories)
    n_protocols = len(protocols)
    scales = case["prior_scales"]
    sampling = case["sampling"]

    with pm.Model():
        grand_mean = pm.Normal("grand_mean", mu=0.0, sigma=scales["grand_mean"])
        laboratory_effect = pm.ZeroSumNormal(
            "laboratory_effect",
            sigma=scales["laboratory"],
            shape=n_laboratories,
        )
        protocol_effect = pm.ZeroSumNormal(
            "protocol_effect",
            sigma=scales["protocol"],
            shape=n_protocols,
        )
        interaction_effect = pm.ZeroSumNormal(
            "interaction_effect",
            sigma=scales["interaction"],
            shape=(n_laboratories, n_protocols),
            n_zerosum_axes=2,
        )
        fitted_response = (
            grand_mean
            + laboratory_effect[:, None]
            + protocol_effect[None, :]
            + interaction_effect
        )
        pm.Normal(
            "observed_cell_summary",
            mu=fitted_response,
            sigma=case["cell_standard_errors"],
            observed=case["cell_estimates"],
        )
        inference_data = pm.sample(
            draws=sampling["draws"],
            tune=sampling["tune"],
            chains=sampling["chains"],
            cores=sampling["cores"],
            random_seed=sampling["seed"],
            target_accept=sampling["target_accept"],
            progressbar=False,
            compute_convergence_checks=False,
            discard_tuned_samples=True,
            return_inferencedata=True,
        )

    posterior = inference_data.posterior
    grand_values = flatten_posterior(np, posterior, "grand_mean", ())
    laboratory_values = flatten_posterior(
        np,
        posterior,
        "laboratory_effect",
        (n_laboratories,),
    )
    protocol_values = flatten_posterior(
        np,
        posterior,
        "protocol_effect",
        (n_protocols,),
    )
    interaction_values = flatten_posterior(
        np,
        posterior,
        "interaction_effect",
        (n_laboratories, n_protocols),
    )

    sample_count = grand_values.shape[0]
    if not (
        laboratory_values.shape[0]
        == protocol_values.shape[0]
        == interaction_values.shape[0]
        == sample_count
    ):
        raise RuntimeError("posterior variables contain inconsistent sample counts")

    fitted_values = (
        grand_values[:, None, None]
        + laboratory_values[:, :, None]
        + protocol_values[:, None, :]
        + interaction_values
    )
    if not np.all(np.isfinite(fitted_values)):
        raise RuntimeError("reconstructed fitted responses contain non-finite values")

    constraint_residuals = {
        "laboratory_effect": float(np.max(np.abs(np.sum(laboratory_values, axis=1)))),
        "protocol_effect": float(np.max(np.abs(np.sum(protocol_values, axis=1)))),
        "interaction_over_laboratories": float(
            np.max(np.abs(np.sum(interaction_values, axis=1)))
        ),
        "interaction_over_protocols": float(
            np.max(np.abs(np.sum(interaction_values, axis=2)))
        ),
    }
    max_constraint_residual = max(constraint_residuals.values())
    constraints_finite = bool(np.isfinite(max_constraint_residual))

    contrast_results = []
    for contrast in case["planned_contrasts"]:
        values = np.zeros(sample_count, dtype=float)
        public_terms = []
        for term in contrast["terms"]:
            values += (
                term["coefficient"]
                * fitted_values[
                    :,
                    term["laboratory_index"],
                    term["protocol_index"],
                ]
            )
            public_terms.append(
                {
                    "laboratory": term["laboratory"],
                    "protocol": term["protocol"],
                    "coefficient": term["coefficient"],
                }
            )

        posterior_summary = summarize_contrast(np, values)
        contrast_results.append(
            {
                "name": contrast["name"],
                "terms": public_terms,
                "posterior_summary": posterior_summary,
            }
        )

    workflow_completed = bool(
        sample_count >= 2
        and np.all(np.isfinite(fitted_values))
        and constraints_finite
        and all(
            np.isfinite(summary["mean"]) and np.isfinite(summary["sd"])
            for result in contrast_results
            for summary in [result["posterior_summary"]]
        )
    )
    status = "workflow_completed" if workflow_completed else "pre_fix_expected_failure"
    return {
        "case_name": case["case_name"],
        "model": {
            "laboratories": laboratories,
            "protocols": protocols,
            "observed_cells": n_laboratories * n_protocols,
            "prior_scales": scales,
        },
        "sampling": {
            "sample_count": int(sample_count),
            "draws": sampling["draws"],
            "tune": sampling["tune"],
            "seed": sampling["seed"],
        },
        "constraints": {
            "residuals": constraint_residuals,
            "maximum_residual": max_constraint_residual,
            "finite": constraints_finite,
        },
        "planned_contrasts": contrast_results,
        "status": status,
    }

        "schema_version": "0.3",
        "offline": True,
        "status_contract": {

        json.dumps(report, indent=2, sort_keys=True) + "\n",
        encoding="utf-8",
    )
    print(json.dumps(report, indent=2, sort_keys=True))
    return 0 if report["status"] == "workflow_completed" else 1

class ZeroSumNormal(Distribution):
    r"""
    ZeroSumNormal distribution, i.e Normal distribution where one or
    several axes are constrained to sum to zero.
    By default, the last axis is constrained to sum to zero.
    See `n_zerosum_axes` kwarg for more details.

    .. math::

        \begin{align*}
            ZSN(\sigma) = N \Big( 0, \sigma^2 (I - \tfrac{1}{n}J) \Big) \\
            \text{where} \ ~ J_{ij} = 1 \ ~ \text{and} \\
            n = \text{nbr of zero-sum axes}
        \end{align*}

    Parameters
    ----------
    sigma : tensor_like of float
        Scale parameter (sigma > 0).
        It's actually the standard deviation of the underlying, unconstrained Normal distribution.
        Defaults to 1 if not specified.
        For now, ``sigma`` has to be a scalar, to ensure the zero-sum constraint.
    n_zerosum_axes: int, defaults to 1
        Number of axes along which the zero-sum constraint is enforced, starting from the rightmost position.
        Defaults to 1, i.e the rightmost axis.
    zerosum_axes: int, deprecated please use n_zerosum_axes as its successor
    dims: sequence of strings, optional
        Dimension names of the distribution. Works the same as for other PyMC distributions.
        Necessary if ``shape`` is not passed.
    shape: tuple of integers, optional
        Shape of the distribution. Works the same as for other PyMC distributions.
        Necessary if ``dims`` or ``observed`` is not passed.

    Warnings
    --------
    ``sigma`` has to be a scalar, to ensure the zero-sum constraint.
    The ability to specify a vector of ``sigma`` may be added in future versions.

    ``n_zerosum_axes`` has to be > 0. If you want the behavior of ``n_zerosum_axes = 0``,
    just use ``pm.Normal``.

    Examples
    --------
    Define a `ZeroSumNormal` variable, with `sigma=1` and
    `n_zerosum_axes=1`  by default::

        COORDS = {
            "regions": ["a", "b", "c"],
            "answers": ["yes", "no", "whatever", "don't understand question"],
        }
        with pm.Model(coords=COORDS) as m:
            # the zero sum axis will be 'answers'
            v = pm.ZeroSumNormal("v", dims=("regions", "answers"))

        with pm.Model(coords=COORDS) as m:
            # the zero sum axes will be 'answers' and 'regions'
            v = pm.ZeroSumNormal("v", dims=("regions", "answers"), n_zerosum_axes=2)

        with pm.Model(coords=COORDS) as m:
            # the zero sum axes will be the last two

# Running the test suite
The first step to run tests is the installation of additional dependencies that are needed for testing:

```bash
pip install -r requirements-dev.txt
```

The PyMC test suite uses `pytest` as the testing framework.
If you are unfamiliar with `pytest`, check out [this short video series](https://calmcode.io/pytest/introduction.html).

With the optional dependencies installed, you can start running tests.
Below are some example of how you might want to run certain parts of the test suite.

```{attention}
Running the entire test suite will take hours.
Therefore, we recommend to run just specific tests that target the parts of the codebase you're working on.
```

To run all tests from a single file:
```bash
pytest -v tests/test_model.py
```

```{tip}
The `-v` flag is short-hand for `--verbose` and prints the names of the test cases that are currently running.
```

Often, you'll want to focus on just a few test cases first.
By using the `-k` flag, you can filter for test cases that match a certain pattern.
For example, the following command runs all test cases from `test_model.py` that have "coord" in their name:

```bash
pytest -v tests/test_model.py -k coord
```


To get a coverage report, you can pass `--cov=pymc`, optionally with `--cov-report term-missing` to get a printout of the line numbers that were visited by the invoked tests.
Note that because you are not running the entire test suite, the coverage will be terrible.
But you can still watch for specific line numbers of the code that you're working on.

```bash
pytest -v --cov=pymc --cov-report term-missing tests/<name of test>.py
```

When you are reasonably confident about the changes you made, you can push the changes and open a pull request.
Our GitHub Actions pipeline will run the entire test suite and if there are failures you can go back and run these tests on your local machine.

        for violated_axis in range(len(support_shape)):
